<explanation>
This project is a Kubernetes-native ingress controller that uses Envoy as the data plane. In broad strokes, it works as the control plane for updating and managing dynamic configuration for an Envoy proxy through the Kubernetes APIs (including Ingress, HTTPProxy CRDs, and Gateway API resources). The project is written in Go and is organized into many modules: command-line tools (in the cmd directory), internal libraries (internal/*), API definitions (apis/*), tests (test/*), documentation (site, docs, design), and examples. The following steps and guidelines will help you create a highly detailed and accurate system design diagram for the Contour project:

1. Identify and outline the core components:
   • Kubernetes Cluster: This is the environment where Contour runs. It provides the API server, kube-controller-manager, and other Kubernetes primitives.
   • Contour Controller: Draw this as the central control component. This includes the main binary (cmd/contour) and its supporting packages for managing configuration, building the DAG (in internal/dag/*), processing CRDs (apis/projectcontour/* and internal/provisioner) and managing state.
   • Envoy Proxy: Represent the Envoy proxy as an external data plane component which receives configuration updates from Contour via the xDS API (see the internal/xds and internal/xdscache directories for details).
   • Configuration APIs:
   – Ingress API (standard Kubernetes Ingress objects)
   – HTTPProxy (Contour’s own CRD with enhanced features)
   – Gateway API (newer, evolving Kubernetes API)
   • Supporting Components: Include ancillary components like the certificate generator (cmd/contour/certgen and internal/certgen), logging, metrics collection modules (internal/metrics), and health checks (internal/health) within Contour.
   • Testing and CI/CD Pipelines: While not part of runtime architecture, note that robust unit and e2e tests, along with CI pipelines (see .github/workflows, test/e2e) are used to ensure system correctness.

2. Define relationships and system interactions:
   • Contour continuously monitors the Kubernetes API for changes in Ingress, HTTPProxy, and Gateway API resources.
   • When a change is detected, Contour’s reconciliation loop (using internal/k8s and internal/dag) rebuilds its internal Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG), reflecting desired routing, TLS, and load balancing policies.
   • This new state is then converted into configuration resources (using xDS protocols, as found in internal/xds and internal/xdscache) which are then pushed to one or more Envoy proxy instances.
   • The Envoy proxy, running as a separate container or deployment, receives configuration updates dynamically and serves as the actual reverse proxy and load balancer for incoming traffic.
   • The diagram should show directional data flows:
  – From Kubernetes API to Contour Controller (watching for resource changes)
  – From Contour Controller to Envoy (pushing xDS configuration updates)
  – Backward or bidirectional communication for health checks and metrics (e.g., Prometheus scraping, as noted in examples and test/e2e/prometheus)
   
3. Highlight key architectural patterns and design principles:
   • Event-driven reconciliation: The control loop is based on watching API events and re-building the routing DAG.
   • Separation of concerns: There is a clear distinction between the control plane (Contour) and the data plane (Envoy) with well-defined API contracts (xDS).
   • Modular design: By splitting functionality across packages (e.g., certgen, dag building, envoy configuration, CRD management), the project makes it easier to extend and test.
   • Extensibility: Multiple APIs (Ingress, HTTPProxy, Gateway API) are supported to give users flexibility in how they define routing.

4. Tailor the diagram to the specifics of this full-stack Kubernetes-based controller:
   • Use clear, distinct shapes (for example, rectangles for components like “Contour Controller”, and cylinders for “Kubernetes API Server” or “Envoy Proxy”).
   • Use directional arrows to show flow:
  – Arrow from “Kubernetes API Server” to “Contour Controller” indicating resource watch events.
  – Arrow from “Contour Controller” to “Envoy Proxy” representing configuration updates through xDS.
  – Arrows indicating control feedback loops (health-checks, metrics collection).
   • Highlight technology details:
  – Mention that the controller is written in Go and uses custom resource definitions (CRDs) for HTTPProxy and Gateway API.
  – Note that Envoy is the reverse proxy utilized.
   • Color-code differences:
  – Use one color or shape style to represent control-plane components (Contour, Kubernetes API server) and another for the data plane (Envoy).
  – Optionally, designate testing/infrastructure components (CI workflows, e2e tests) using a different style to show they do not run in production but are essential for quality assurance.

5. Provide instructions for creating the diagram:
   • Start by drawing the Kubernetes cluster as the environment.
   • Inside the cluster, depict “Contour Controller” and list sub-components or mention internal modules (CRD processing, DAG builder, xDS configuration generator) as sub-blocks if needed.
   • Illustrate the connection from the Kubernetes API Server feeding events/changes to the Contour Controller.
   • Represent the Envoy proxy as an independently managed data plane component, receiving configuration updates from the controller.
   • Add labels to indicate supported APIs (Ingress, HTTPProxy, Gateway API) and show them feeding into the Contour Controller.
   • Use directional arrows to detail the flow of configuration data (for example, “resource change event –> reconcile DAG –> push xDS configuration”).
   • Optionally, include monitoring/observability components like Prometheus and logging aggregation if detailing operational aspects.
   • Ensure the diagram is detailed yet readable—do not add extraneous detail, but capture each major component and the flow of information between them.

In summary, your system design diagram should explicitly capture:
   • The separation between the Kubernetes API, Contour’s control logic (including its internal DAG builder, CRD processors, and xDS configuration generator), and the Envoy data plane.
   • The multi-API support (Ingress, HTTPProxy, Gateway API) as entry-points for configuration.
   • The dynamic, event-driven update process and the modular design of the software.
By following these guidelines, your diagram will accurately represent the architectural design of Contour and provide clarity on how requests flow through the system from Kubernetes-managed resources to Envoy proxy configurations.
</explanation>
